games.title: Tank
games.note: Two players steer tanks through a minefield maze. Kee Games was an Atari offshoot that posed as a rival company.

games.title: Battlezone
games.note: Wireframe tank battles seen through a periscope-style viewer. Atari also built a modified version as a US Army training aid.

games.title: MIDI Maze
games.note: Up to 16 Atari STs could be chained through their MIDI music ports for deathmatches between smiley faces. Later ported as Faceball 2000.

games.title: Hovertank 3D
games.note: John Carmack's first first-person engine, made for the Softdisk subscription service. John Romero voiced the sound effects himself.

games.title: Pathways into Darkness
games.note: Bungie's first 3D game: a first-person shooter-adventure inside a pyramid where an alien god sleeps.

games.title: Marathon
games.note: Told its story through computer terminals where three AIs talk to you, and offered eight-player network deathmatch on Macs.

games.title: Magic Carpet
games.note: You fly a carpet over 3D landscapes that spells can reshape, collecting mana into castles you build.

games.title: Heretic
games.note: A dark-fantasy shooter on a licensed Doom engine, with an inventory of magic items and the ability to fly.

games.title: Hexen
games.note: Full title Hexen: Beyond Heretic. Fighter, cleric and mage classes, and hub levels where switches change distant areas.

games.title: Star Wars: Dark Forces
games.note: Introduced mercenary Kyle Katarn. Its Dark Troopers later became canon in The Mandalorian.

games.title: Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II
games.note: Added lightsaber duels and Force powers, with live-action video cutscenes between levels.

games.title: Duke Nukem 3D
games.note: Built on Ken Silverman's Build engine. Most props can be smashed, and its source code was released in 2003.

games.title: Team Fortress
games.note: A free Quake mod by two Australians, with classes like Medic and Sniper. Valve hired them in 1998.

games.title: Team Fortress Classic
games.note: A port of the Quake mod to Half-Life, released by Valve as a free mod.

games.title: Team Fortress 2
games.note: Shipped in The Orange Box after nine years in development. Its look draws on J. C. Leyendecker and Norman Rockwell.

games.title: Virtua Cop
games.note: A 3D light-gun shooter where criminals react to where each bullet hits them.

games.title: GoldenEye 007
games.note: Began as a planned on-rails shooter. Its four-player split-screen deathmatch made the case for shooters on consoles.

games.title: Myth: The Fallen Lords
games.note: Real-time tactics with no base building: you command a small army across 3D terrain.

games.title: Perfect Dark
games.note: Rare's spiritual successor to GoldenEye, with agent Joanna Dark and computer-controlled bots called Simulants in multiplayer.

games.title: TimeSplitters
games.note: A PlayStation 2 launch game from ex-GoldenEye developers who founded Free Radical in Nottingham. It included a level editor.

games.title: TimeSplitters 2
games.note: Time-hopping missions from 1930s Chicago to a Siberian dam that nods to GoldenEye.

games.title: Syphon Filter
games.note: Agent Gabe Logan's taser became famous: hold the trigger long enough and the target catches fire.

games.title: Half-Life: Opposing Force
games.note: Gearbox's first game: the Black Mesa disaster seen by Adrian Shephard, a Marine sent to cover it up.

games.title: Daikatana
games.note: John Romero's first game after leaving id. Years of delays and a boastful magazine ad made it a cautionary tale.

games.title: Serious Sam: The First Encounter
games.note: Croatian studio Croteam threw hundreds of enemies at once at the player in huge open Egyptian arenas.

games.title: Red Faction
games.note: Its Geo-Mod engine let you blow holes through walls and rock to make your own paths on a Mars mining colony.

games.title: WinBack
games.note: A third-person shooter built around taking cover at corners and leaning out to shoot, with laser sights on every gun.

games.title: kill.switch
games.note: Added blind fire: shooting from behind cover without looking. Lead designer Chris Esaki later worked on Gears of War.

games.title: Bionic Commando
games.note: You cannot jump; a mechanical arm swings you across gaps. The 1988 NES game is a different, larger take.

games.title: Loaded
games.note: A gory top-down shooter for the early PlayStation. Remedy's first idea for Max Payne grew from it.

games.title: The Chronicles of Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay
games.note: A film tie-in made in Uppsala that mixed stealth, fistfights and shooting, co-developed with Vin Diesel's Tigon Studios.

games.title: Garry's Mod
games.note: Began as a free Half-Life 2 sandbox mod, sold on Steam from 2006. Newman later said it should have been called Sandbox.

games.title: F.E.A.R.
games.note: Its soldiers plan their own moves with goal-oriented action planning, an AI system written by engineer Jeff Orkin.

games.title: Crysis
games.note: So demanding on PCs that 'But can it run Crysis?' became a long-running joke.

games.title: Metro 2033
games.note: Based on Dmitry Glukhovsky's novel about survivors in Moscow's metro after a nuclear war. Military-grade bullets serve as money.

games.title: Dusk
games.note: A 1990s-style shooter published by New Blood, with three episodes, an endless mode and multiplayer.

games.title: Ultrakill
games.note: Made largely by one Finnish developer. You heal by standing in your enemies' blood, so attacking keeps you alive.

games.title: Day of Defeat
games.dev: Day of Defeat team (mod), later Valve
games.note: A World War II team shooter that began as a free Half-Life mod; Valve released it commercially in 2003.

games.title: Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory
games.note: Planned as a paid expansion, then released free as a multiplayer game when its single-player part was dropped.

links.took: Tank-versus-tank combat; designer Ed Rotberg was mainly inspired by Atari's Tank.
links.added: Turned the top-down duel into a first-person wireframe 3D battlefield seen through a periscope.
links.extra: Rotberg doubted that the PLATO tank game Panther played a part; he never played it.

links.took: Battlezone popularized first-person 3D vehicle combat, which Hovertank 3D is built around.
links.added: Solid-colored walls on an ordinary PC, and civilians to rescue before a bomb drops.
links.extra: No documented direct link: Carmack favored fast action like Gauntlet, and the team loved Wing Commander.

links.took: Players hunting each other through a first-person maze across a network.
links.added: Ran on Atari STs linked by MIDI cables, with up to 16 players as smiley faces.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Maze had little influence on later shooters; Catacomb 3-D arose independently.

links.took: First-person 3D space flight, which Spasim offered on the PLATO network in 1974.
links.added: Trading and open-ended travel across a galaxy, on a home computer.
links.extra: Wikipedia calls Spasim a 'spiritual ancestor' of Elite, not a direct influence.

links.took: Carmack's first-person engine from Hovertank 3D, which served as a prototype.
links.added: Texture-mapped walls and a hand that throws fireballs, a step toward Wolfenstein 3D.

links.took: The 3D engine Bungie built for Pathways into Darkness.
links.added: A sci-fi shooter with mouse aiming, network deathmatch and a story told through terminals.

links.took: Fast first-person shooting through corridors and open rooms, as Doom had shown on PC.
links.added: Mouse free-look, eight-player network games and a long story read on computer terminals.
links.extra: Gaming historians called it 'the Macintosh's answer to the PC's Doom'.

links.took: Bungie's shooter heritage; Jason Jones called the first plan 'the natural extension of Marathon'.
links.added: Vehicles, recharging shields and a two-gun limit, built for a console controller.
links.extra: Cortana continues Marathon's idea of an AI guiding an armed hero.

links.took: Halo began as a sci-fi strategy game built on the Myth engine.
links.added: It became a third-person action game, then a first-person shooter for Microsoft's Xbox.

links.took: Console first-person shooting and split-screen deathmatch, which GoldenEye proved could work.
links.added: Twin-stick controls, vehicles, and linked Xboxes for 16-player games.
links.extra: Edge said GoldenEye set the standard for console multiplayer until Halo arrived in 2001.

links.took: The idea came from Doom fan mods that put levels on the Death Star.
links.added: Its own Jedi engine with jumping, looking up and down, multi-floor levels and puzzles.

links.took: Kyle Katarn and Dark Forces' Star Wars shooting.
links.added: Lightsaber fights, Force powers with light and dark paths, and live-action cutscenes.

links.took: Doom popularized the fast first-person shooter that Duke Nukem 3D is built around.
links.added: Real-world places like cinemas and city streets, breakable props, and a wisecracking hero.

links.took: id's Doom engine, licensed to Raven Software.
links.added: Dark fantasy, an inventory of magic items, and flight.

links.took: Raven's dark-fantasy world and Doom-engine shooting.
links.added: Three character classes and hub worlds with puzzles spread across linked levels.

links.took: Shoot-everything survival; Romero and Carmack both named Space Invaders their introduction to games.
links.added: Moved the fight into first-person 3D mazes full of demons, with network deathmatch.
links.extra: Scholar Frans Mäyrä compared both games' challenge of 'shooting everything that moves'.

links.took: Doom popularized deathmatch; Quake III Arena is built entirely around it.
links.added: No story campaign: bot matches, arena maps, rocket jumps and fast online duels.

links.took: Built as a free mod on Quake's engine and online play.
links.added: Classes such as Medic, Sniper and Engineer working as a team, plus headshots.

links.took: The same mod, rebuilt by its creators after Valve hired them in 1998.
links.added: Released free as Valve's official Half-Life mod in 1999.

links.took: Valve's class-based team shooter, reworked over nine years.
links.added: Nine cartoon characters with big personalities, inspired by 20th-century commercial illustration.
links.extra: Wikipedia calls it the main forerunner of the hero shooter genre.

links.took: Built as a mod on Half-Life's engine, like Counter-Strike.
links.added: World War II objective battles between Allied and Axis classes, later sold by Valve.

links.took: Return to Castle Wolfenstein's engine and team multiplayer, as a planned expansion.
links.added: Free objective battles with five classes, from London studio Splash Damage.

links.took: Reloading, enemies reacting to where they're hit, and penalties for shooting innocents.
links.added: Free movement through 3D levels with mission objectives instead of a fixed path.

src.t: Engadget, Richard Mitchell (Martin Hollis at GDC Europe), Sep 2012

links.extra: GoldenEye began as an on-rails shooter in the Virtua Cop mold.

links.took: Free-roaming first-person shooting; Hollis pictured play somewhere between Virtua Cop and Doom.
links.added: Stealth, location-based hits, a zooming sniper rifle and four-player split-screen.

src.t: Engadget, Richard Mitchell (Martin Hollis at GDC Europe), Sep 2012

links.took: Several tasks per stage, which inspired GoldenEye's multi-objective missions.
links.added: Extra objectives that appear on harder difficulty settings, in a spy-film setting.
links.extra: Mario 64's 3D collision system also influenced Hollis.

links.took: Rare's GoldenEye team and an upgraded version of its engine.
links.added: An original sci-fi spy story, co-op missions and computer-controlled bots in multiplayer.

links.took: Former GoldenEye developers, plus its health display and aiming style.
links.added: A fast arcade shooter jumping between eras, with a built-in level editor.

links.took: Free Radical's time-hopping arcade shooting.
links.added: A full story mode, many more characters, and a dam level nodding to GoldenEye.

links.took: Steven Spielberg watched his son Max play GoldenEye and wanted a World War II shooter.
links.added: Missions advised by Captain Dale Dye and an orchestral score by Michael Giacchino.

src.t: GamesRadar+, The Making Of Medal of Honor

links.extra: The idea came while Spielberg was making Saving Private Ryan.

links.took: Varied mission objectives and alert, reactive enemy soldiers.
links.added: A continuous story with no cutscenes, and Marines who flank and throw grenades.
links.extra: Wikipedia names Half-Life, Thief, Syphon Filter and Deus Ex as influenced by its missions and AI.

links.took: Stealth as an option inside a first-person game.
links.added: Made stealth the whole game, with light, shadow and noise deciding if you are seen.

links.took: Missions you could finish quietly or loudly.
links.added: Skill and augmentation choices, conversations, and several routes through every level.

links.took: Stealthy spy missions with varied objectives.
links.added: A third-person view, a rolling dodge and a taser that sets enemies alight.

links.took: Its lead developers, who left 2015 Inc. and formed Infinity Ward in 2002.
links.added: Allied soldiers fighting beside you, plus British and Soviet campaigns alongside the American one.

src.t: GamesRadar+, How the war began: the making of Call of Duty

links.extra: The project's early nickname was 'Medal of Honor Killer'.

links.took: An enhanced id Tech 3 engine, originally built for Quake III Arena.
links.added: Its own animation system, and squadmates who flank, suppress and move between cover.

links.took: id Tech 3, the Quake III Arena engine.
links.added: Scripted, film-like World War II set pieces such as the Omaha Beach landing.

src.t: Wikipedia: Medal of Honor: Allied Assault

links.took: Founders Jason West and Vince Zampella and many former Infinity Ward developers.
links.added: Wall-running pilots and giant Titans in online matches with AI-controlled grunts.
links.extra: Activision fired West and Zampella after Modern Warfare 2; they founded Respawn in 2010.

links.took: Valve's Source engine, and wall-running that began as a programmer's Half-Life 2 mod.
links.added: Parkour across rooftops and calling down a mech, at 60 frames per second.

links.took: The scrapped Doom 4 borrowed Call of Duty's cover, regenerating health and scripted scenes.
links.added: id restarted in 2011; the final game rewards charging forward instead of hiding.
links.extra: Developers and fans mocked the scrapped version as 'Call of Doom'.

links.took: The original's speed, demons and art; Marty Stratton said id wanted to honor its legacy.
links.added: Glory kills and chainsaw kills that refill health and ammo, so attacking keeps you alive.

links.took: Sweeping 3D terrain; James Schmalz began Unreal with 'a Magic Carpet-type terrain'.
links.added: Tim Sweeney's Unreal Engine, colored lighting and huge indoor-outdoor levels.

links.took: The Unreal Engine, licensed by Ion Storm.
links.added: Role-playing choices, augmentations and several routes through a near-future conspiracy.

links.took: Epic's Unreal team; Gears began as 'Unreal Warfare', paused while Epic made Unreal Tournament.
links.added: A cover-based third-person campaign with two-player co-op, on Unreal Engine 3.
links.extra: The first concept was much closer to the multiplayer-driven Unreal games.

links.took: The tactical cover system, which lead designer Cliff Bleszinski credited.
links.added: One-button snap into cover, the roadie run, active reloads and a chainsaw bayonet.
links.extra: kill.switch lead designer Chris Esaki later worked on Gears at Epic.

links.took: The over-the-shoulder camera and tight pacing, which Bleszinski cited.
links.added: Put that view into a cover-based war shooter with two-player co-op.

src.t: GameSpot, GDC 2007: Cliff Bleszinski on Gears

links.took: The rhythm of swinging between platforms, which Bleszinski likened to moving cover to cover.
links.added: Turned that rhythm into sprinting and sliding between cover under fire.

links.took: Bleszinski cited its world-building, tool mastery and underground spaces.
links.added: Locust tunnels under a ruined planet, explored as the squad pushes underground.

links.took: The name: 'Gears of War' is a homage to Metal Gear, an early influence on Bleszinski.
links.added: Little of the stealth: a loud, cover-based shooter about soldiers holding the line.

links.took: Its cover system, which lead designers Evan Wells and Amy Hennig credited.
links.added: Climbing, puzzles and a pulp treasure hunt between cover-based firefights.

links.took: Third-person cover with blind fire around corners.
links.added: Switches to first person to aim, with squad orders in Las Vegas casinos.

links.took: Ducking behind corners and leaning out to shoot.
links.added: Blind fire and a fuller cover system, later seen as a base for modern shooters.

links.took: Corner cover and laser sights on guns.
links.added: Stealth-first infiltration with first-person aiming and guards who search as a team.

links.took: Laser sights on guns, which Wikipedia says Resident Evil 4 adopted.
links.added: Over-the-shoulder aiming that hits specific body parts, staggering enemies.

links.took: A third-person 3D action game; Remedy wanted one, minus its 'horrid camera system'.
links.added: Bullet time, slow-motion dives and a noir story told in graphic-novel panels.

links.took: Remedy's first idea for an action game grew from this top-down shooter.
links.added: Moved to a third-person 3D view with Hong Kong action-film gunfights.

links.took: Max Payne popularized slow-motion gunfights; F.E.A.R. builds its combat around 'reflex time'.
links.added: Squads that flank and take cover, plus Japanese-style horror.
links.extra: Lead designer Craig Hubbard cited the film Hard Boiled, not Max Payne.

links.took: Remedy and writer Sam Lake's narrated, story-first action.
links.added: A horror thriller where you burn away darkness with a flashlight before shooting.

links.took: Goal-oriented action planning, where enemies pick goals and plan their actions live.
links.added: Used it in an open Chernobyl zone with mutants and rival stalkers.
links.extra: Wikipedia lists S.T.A.L.K.E.R. among later games that used this AI approach.

links.took: Former GSC Game World staff, including most of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. art team.
links.added: A tightly scripted story in Moscow's metro tunnels, with gas masks and makeshift guns.

links.took: Atmosphere-first storytelling in an unbroken first-person view, largely inspired by Half-Life 2.
links.added: Ammunition as money, gas-mask filters that run out, and survival in tunnels.

links.took: Abstract, non-linear levels shaped by John Romero's Doom maps; Szymanski grew up on Doom.
links.added: Faster movement with flips and slides, and backwoods horror settings.

links.took: Quake's chunky low-polygon look, which David Szymanski set out to copy.
links.added: A full three-episode campaign plus an endless mode and online multiplayer.

links.took: Abandoned industrial areas, which inspired Dusk's second episode.
links.added: Filled them with cultists and soldiers in a fast retro shooter.

links.took: Combo attacks and a style meter that rewards fighting with flair.
links.added: Put them in a first-person shooter where you heal from enemies' blood.

links.took: Fast, aggressive movement through combat arenas.
links.added: Dashing, sliding, and punching enemy projectiles back at them.
links.extra: Wikipedia also cites Titanfall for its modern movement.

links.took: Built as a mod for Half-Life 2 on Valve's Source engine and physics.
links.added: No goals: a sandbox for spawning and welding objects, which players turned into new modes.
links.extra: Player-made modes like Prop Hunt later appeared in Fortnite and Call of Duty.

links.took: Same studio: Garry's Mod's success let Facepunch grow and make other games.
links.added: Open-world survival with gathering, crafting and raiding other players' bases.

links.took: Crytek's engine work after Far Cry, which EA commissioned and which led to Crysis.
links.added: A nanosuit switching between strength, speed, armor and cloaking in an open jungle.

links.took: Irrational Games and Ken Levine's System Shock 2 formula: audio logs, upgrades, a ruined place.
links.added: An underwater art deco city, plasmid powers, and a twist about free will.

links.took: Seven former Starbreeze developers, from the studio behind Riddick, founded MachineGames in 2009.
links.added: A story-heavy Wolfenstein where most fights can be played with stealth or force.
links.extra: MachineGames is based in Uppsala, Sweden.

links.took: Half-Life's world and the Black Mesa disaster.
links.added: Seen as Marine Adrian Shephard, with new weapons, allies and alien enemies.

links.took: Gearbox Software, which began on Half-Life expansions before making its own games.
links.added: A co-op shooter with procedurally generated guns and role-playing progression.

src.t: PC Gamer, From Half-Life to Borderlands: the rise of Gearbox Software

links.took: The moment-to-moment fun of shooting, which Randy Pitchford traced to Wolfenstein 3D.
links.added: Role-playing growth on top: levels, skill trees and endless loot.

links.took: The steady stream of loot that keeps you playing, per Randy Pitchford.
links.added: Moved that loot loop into a four-player co-op first-person shooter.
links.extra: Pitchford called it a 'role-playing shooter'.

links.took: Console shooting feel; Pitchford pitched Borderlands as 'Halo and Diablo put together'.
links.added: Cel-shaded art and four-player co-op across an open desert planet.

src.t: Shacknews, Randy Pitchford, Borderlands E3 interview

links.took: Bungie's team and shooting feel, which moved on after Halo: Reach.
links.added: A persistent online world with loot, raids and public events.

links.took: Exploration and long-term investment like World of Warcraft, per executive producer Patrick O'Kelley.
links.added: Combined with Bungie's first-person combat on consoles.

src.t: Game Developer, Luke Smith on WoW and Destiny raids, May 2017

links.extra: Destiny 2 director Luke Smith later said WoW also inspired its raids.

links.took: Borderlands set the looter-shooter mold: guns with random stats and rarity tiers.
links.added: MMO elements such as raids, clans and a social hub, which broadened the genre.

links.took: The Quake II engine, licensed by John Romero's Ion Storm after he left id.
links.added: Time travel across four eras with two AI sidekicks, a source of much frustration.

links.took: Doom popularized the run-and-gun shooter; Serious Sam scales it up.
links.added: Hundreds of enemies charging at once across huge open arenas.

src.t: Wikipedia: Serious Sam: The First Encounter
